..
Issued at 133 AM CST Tue Nov 24 2026

Recent RAP-analyzed surface fields and GOES-19 water vapor 
imagery depict a 1036 mb surface high pressure system centered 
along the Minnesota and Iowa borders beneath an implied short- 
wavelength upper-level ridge. Mostly clear skies early this 
morning on the eastern side of the surface high have allowed 
for a land breeze to develop across northeastern Illinois. When 
paired with a weak inverted surface trough in Lower Michigan 
(leading to easterly winds), a zone of focused low-level 
confluence is gradually intensifying over southern Lake 
Michigan. In spite of marginal inversion heights, do still 
anticipate a lake effect snow shower or two to develop within 
the convergence zone this morning which would be poised to graze
the northwestern Indiana and eventually northeastern Illinois 
shoreline. Our expectation remains for no accumulations of snow 
with the morning. 

Outside any localized lake effect snow showers of stratocumulus
clouds near the lakeshore this morning, upper-level cloud cover
will gradually increase throughout the day. High temperatures 
today look quite similar to yesterday and generally in the lower
40s. Wednesday looks similar with mostly cloudy skies and highs
in the lower 40s. 

Attention then turns to what is shaping up to be a busy 
Wednesday night through Friday timeframe across the eastern 
United States. Ensemble model guidance remains in excellent 
agreement that a northern-stream upper-level wave will dive 
south across the Plains Wednesday and phase with a pseudo- 
subtropical wave meandering along the Gulf Coast on Thursday. 
The net result will be an unusual pathway to the development of 
a sprawling low pressure system along the Atlantic coast with an
elongated surface low pressure trough extending westward into 
the Lower Great Lakes beneath the phased upper-level low. The 
large storm system would then be poised to lift northeastward 
into eastern Canada on Friday along the northeastern edge of a 
combined 150kt polar/subtropical jet extending into the north 
Atlantic. While the big-picture idea has remained consistent for
several days now, there remains spread in the exact phasing 
evolution of the waves within the ensemble envelope. As a 
result, adjustments in the forecast may continue in the next 24 
to 36 hours. 

Generally speaking, increasing (easterly!) low-level warm air 
advection should facilitate the rapid development of a north-to-
south oriented band of precipitation in the middle Mississippi 
River Valley by Wednesday night. Individual ensemble QPF postage
stamps from the EPS and GEFS show locations of the initial WAA 
band as far west as the Mississippi River to as far east as the 
Indiana/Illinois border, with a general consensus smack dab in 
the middle (near the I-39 corridor). Cooling mid-level 
temperatures by virtue of rising synoptic-scale motion within an
unusually-oriented coupled jet structure will force 
precipitation type to snow on the western side of the WAA-driven
band leading to slushy accumulations (should end up an oddly- 
oriented snow-band, frankly). Meanwhile, dry easterly flow on 
the southern side of the departing high pressure system may act 
to chew up what would be a cold rain on the northeastern side of
the WAA-driven precipitation band through daybreak Thursday. 
(As a result, there are plays for both the Rockford and Chicago 
metropolitan areas to remain dry through Wednesday night). 

Rain should expand in coverage throughout the day on Thursday 
within a developing expansive west-to-east deformation band (the
primary moisture source will be the Atlantic which is fairly 
atypical for our area). Will again note variance in ensemble 
guidance on the footprint of QPF particularly with northward 
extent, including a healthy grouping that fail to depict 
rainfall north of I-88. Nevertheless, rain will continue across 
at least parts of the area Thursday night into Friday as the low
begins to pull away. By the time the system leaves our area, 
total rainfall amounts may locally approach 2 inches (favored 
near the US-24 corridor), which may lead to ponding in low-lying
areas such as ditches and fields. Taken altogether, Thanksgiving
and the first half of Friday are shaping up to be wet in our 
general region. 

This weekend and beyond, ensemble guidance supports a busy 
weather pattern continuing with additional storm systems moving 
across the central US. Per ensemble meteograms of QPF, am noting
preferred time windows for additional precipitation in the 
November 30th and December 3-5 timeframes. Temperatures are
favored to remain seasonable, though a signal remains for
moderating temperatures by early December. 

Borchardt
